fields.title: Where does retrieval coverage come from? User representations, positive examples, and negative difficulty
fields.thesis: Candidate generation determines what downstream ranking can see. YouTube DNN uses one user vector for nearest-neighbor retrieval; Airbnb EBR ties supervision to the search–browse–booking journey; MIMA allocates multiple positives from a request to complementary interests; MDCNS changes negative difficulty and provides multi-view supervision. These alter representations, labels, interest specialization, and gradients, respectively. More retrieved candidates are not a common explanation.
fields.axis_0: Retrieval interface: single vector or multiple interest channels
fields.axis_1: Positives from next actions, journeys, or same-request sets
fields.axis_2: How negative difficulty and teacher supervision change gradients
fields.axis_3: Fixed candidate budgets and inventory/data substitution limits

fields.position: Aggregates watch history and context into a user vector using a DNN. Trains as large-scale next-video classification, then serves dot-product nearest neighbors against video vectors.
fields.tradeoff: Independent item vectors are indexable; a single user vector must encode multiple interests. Retrieval still has a separate role from ranking. Small public data do not reproduce a million-scale production index.

fields.position: Retains query/item dot-product dual encoders, but constructs positives and hard negatives across searching, browsing, and booking. Traffic replay aligns first-stage retrieval.
fields.tradeoff: Labels better reflect the marketplace journey. Real coverage also depends on geography, inventory updates, and indexing. The local MovieLens proxy cannot validate lodging availability constraints or online gains.

fields.position: A causal decoder emits multiple interests, supervised by one-to-one optimal matching against same-request positives. Interest activation probabilities calibrate channel scores.
fields.tradeoff: Exclusive assignment discourages all positives collapsing into one interest, but depends on real multi-positive sets and routing calibration. Neighboring actions substitute for same-request conversions locally, so this does not establish production interest decomposition.

fields.position: Self, Peer, and Teacher score the candidate pool from multiple views. Model disagreement adjusts hard-negative ranking; the teacher's full-pool soft distribution is distilled into Self.
fields.tradeoff: Adds supervision beyond one high-scoring negative. Hard negatives may still be false negatives, and disagreement does not establish ground truth. Align candidate pools, sampling budgets, and training costs.

fields.title: Locate the bottleneck: coverage, supervision, or interest collapse
fields.body: YouTube DNN compresses history into one user vector. Airbnb EBR keeps a similar retrieval interface but reorganizes journey supervision. A similar dual-encoder shape does not make their training problems equivalent. MIMA's defining change is one-to-one assignment of same-request positives, not merely emitting more vectors; otherwise interests may converge on one positive. Fix the final return budget to separate better representations from retrieving more items.

fields.title: Hard negatives and multiple positives have different roles
fields.body: MDCNS finds unobserved candidates models find difficult and disagree on, giving Self full-pool teacher supervision. MIMA learns interest specialization from real positive sets. Labeling all unclicked items as negatives or treating adjacent behaviors as complementary same-request positives changes the meaning of supervision. Airbnb EBR's journey reminds us to record behavioral stages and exposure before interpreting a lower loss.

fields.question: If recall rises after MIMA returns multiple interests, how can we distinguish complementarity from a larger candidate budget?
fields.answer: Fix total K after merging and deduplicating channels, then compare with single-vector retrieval. Check whether positive assignments and hits complement each other. The mechanism is MIMA's one-to-one supervision and activation calibration; YouTube DNN gives a single-vector starting point. Giving each interest an extra K makes a coverage gain impossible to attribute to interest modeling alone.
fields.example: If running and photography each return 50 items, compare the merged 100-item budget to one channel with 100, not 50.

fields.question: Why do Airbnb EBR and MDCNS emphasize negatives without simply taking the highest-scoring unclicked item as the best negative?
fields.answer: Airbnb interprets hard negatives in their journey and behavioral stage. MDCNS uses disagreement across views rather than only Self's preferences. A non-click can reflect underexposure, substitution, or a missing label. A high score means the current model sees similarity, not that the item is certainly irrelevant. Control false negatives, diversity, and sampling budget.
fields.example: A user booked one property, but two other suitable properties were sold out. Treating them as definitely irrelevant mistakes inventory outcomes for semantic preferences.

fields.question: Why can't a stronger ranker recover an interest missed by retrieval, and where can a new training objective help?
fields.answer: The ranker only sorts existing candidates. YouTube DNN separates the stages; MIMA changes which interests nominate candidates using multi-positive assignments; MDCNS changes the negative gradients received by retrieval representations. Check coverage, fixed-K quality, and downstream ranking separately instead of diagnosing the bottleneck from clicks alone.
fields.example: If all 100 candidates are running shoes, a ranker cannot show a camera. Multi-interest retrieval must nominate the camera before ranking can compare its value with the shoes.

fields.summary: Initial version: compared YouTube DNN, Airbnb EBR, MIMA, and MDCNS. Added analysis and cross-paper questions on retrieval interfaces and next-action, journey, or same-request positives.
